k1p1-2.name: text#2
k1p1-2.text: KP10 One hidden layer can approximate anything

k1p1-15.name: text#15
k1p1-15.text: on a bounded range, approximate any continuous $f$ to any accuracy $\varepsilon$

k1p2-2.name: text#2
k1p2-2.text: It is a “basis”, like Fourier and wavelets

k1p2-17.name: text#17
k1p2-17.text: this kind of theorem is called a representation theorem

k1p3-2.name: text#2
k1p3-2.text: Build one by hand: the staircase

k1p3-17.name: text#17
k1p3-17.text: cut $[0,1]$ into $N=5$ cells; each takes the value at its midpoint

k1p3-19.name: text#19
k1p3-19.text: each step = one very steep sigmoid

k1p3-21.name: text#21
k1p3-21.text:
jumps from 0 to 1 at $t_i$
exactly the form $\sum\alpha_i\sigma(w_ix+\theta_i)$

k1p3-23.name: text#23
k1p3-23.text: the staircase works only in 1-D, but it makes “enough neurons approximate” visible

k1p4-2.name: text#2
k1p4-2.text: The parameters are worked out by hand, not learned

k1p4-21.name: text#21
k1p4-21.text:
$w_i=k$, $\theta_i=-kt_i$, $\alpha_i=v_{i+1}-v_i$
only this 1-D example has such formulas; in general a learning algorithm must find them

k1p4-23.name: text#23
k1p4-23.text: plus a constant term $v_1$, i.e. one more bias

k1p5-2.name: text#2
k1p5-2.text: Double the neurons, roughly halve the error

k1p5-26.name: text#26
k1p5-26.text: half a cell times the maximum slope $2\pi$; $N=10$: $0.309\approx\pi/10$

k1p5-28.name: text#28
k1p5-28.text: an error below $0.01$ needs about $N\approx320$: “enough” may really be a lot

k1p6-2.name: text#2
k1p6-2.text: The proof skeleton of the general theorem (four steps)

k1p6-6.name: text#6
k1p6-6.text: $\mathcal{H}_\sigma=\mathrm{span}\{\sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}+\theta)\}$ must be dense in the continuous functions

k1p6-9.name: text#9
k1p6-9.text: assume not dense $\to$ Hahn–Banach: a nonzero linear functional $L$ vanishes on all of $\mathcal{H}_\sigma$

k1p6-15.name: text#15
k1p6-15.text: continuous, bounded, nonconstant $\sigma$ separates measures, forcing $\mu=0$, contradicting $L\ne0$

k1p6-17.name: text#17
k1p6-17.text: only the skeleton here; the details are functional analysis

k1p7-2.name: text#2
k1p7-2.text: What it guarantees and what it does not

k1p7-7.name: text#7
k1p7-7.text: for large enough $N$, a single-hidden-layer network has parameters that approximate any continuous function to any accuracy

k1p7-11.name: text#11
k1p7-11.text: not promised: how large $N$ must be

k1p7-15.name: text#15
k1p7-15.text: not promised: how to find the parameters (Chapter 3)

k1p7-19.name: text#19
k1p7-19.text: not promised: that it does well on unseen data (KP04's generalization)

k1p7-23.name: text#23
k1p7-23.text: not promised: that training reaches the global optimum

k1p7-25.name: text#25
k1p7-25.text: the theorem promises “a solution exists”, not “it can be found” or “it generalizes”

k1p8-5.name: text#5
k1p8-5.text: “guarantees a network can learn any function”

k1p8-6.name: text#6
k1p8-6.text: no: it only says parameters exist; how to find them, how many, how well they generalize are outside

k1p8-8.name: text#8
k1p8-8.text: “the activation must be a sigmoid or bounded”

k1p8-9.name: text#9
k1p8-9.text: this version assumes bounded; later work shows any non-polynomial works, even ReLU

k1p8-11.name: text#11
k1p8-11.text: “many layers are needed for expressive power”

k1p8-12.name: text#12
k1p8-12.text: one layer suffices for approximation; many layers usually need far fewer neurons

k1p8-14.name: text#14
k1p8-14.text: We know what a network can represent. The real question: how do these weights learn themselves, especially the hidden layers in a deep network that never see the answer?

steps.label: KP10 One hidden layer can approximate anything
What it says · 1/8
steps.speakerNotes: Chapter 2 looked at many models whose common feature is stacked neurons. The question: with a single hidden layer and enough neurons, how many functions can be represented?

steps.label: What it says · 1/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The universal approximation theorem: on a bounded range, a network with one hidden layer of N neurons can approximate any continuous function to any accuracy.

steps.label: What it says · 1/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The condition is that the activation is continuous, bounded and not constant.

steps.label: What it says · 1/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: what \sigma must be continuous, bounded, not constant F(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\alpha_i\,\sigma(\mathbf{w}_i^\top\mathbf{x}+\theta_i) with \sup|f-F|<\varepsilon

steps.label: Representation theorem · 2/8
steps.speakerNotes: A Fourier series approximates functions with trigonometric functions.

steps.label: Representation theorem · 2/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Wavelets approximate with wavelet bases.

steps.label: Representation theorem · 2/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The neural network's sigma of w transpose x plus theta is also a basis. This kind of theorem is a representation theorem.

steps.label: Representation theorem · 2/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: neural network \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}+\theta) approximate with neurons this kind of theorem is called a representation theorem

steps.label: The staircase · 3/8
steps.speakerNotes: Take the one-dimensional sine on 0 to 1.

steps.label: The staircase · 3/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Cut the interval into N cells, here N equals 5, and each cell takes the function value at its midpoint, giving a staircase.

steps.label: The staircase · 3/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Treat a very steep sigmoid as a step jumping from 0 to 1 at t; the staircase is then a weighted sum of sigmas.

steps.label: The staircase · 3/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: each step = one very steep sigmoid \sigma\big(k(x-t_i)\big) jumps from 0 to 1 at t_i exactly the form \sum\alpha_i\sigma(w_ix+\theta_i) the staircase works only in 1-D, but it makes “enough neurons approximate” visible

steps.label: Parameters by hand · 4/8
steps.speakerNotes: With three cells, the three midpoint values are 0.866, 0, minus 0.866.

steps.label: Parameters by hand · 4/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Each step's height alpha is the difference of neighboring cells, here minus 0.866 and minus 0.866.

steps.label: Parameters by hand · 4/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: w equals k, theta equals minus k times t, and alpha is the neighboring difference. These parameters were worked out for the 1-D example; in general no such formula exists and a learning algorithm is needed, which is Chapter 3.

steps.label: Parameters by hand · 4/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: w_i=k, \theta_i=-kt_i, \alpha_i=v_{i+1}-v_i only this 1-D example has such formulas; in general a learning algorithm must find them plus a constant term v_1, i.e. one more bias

steps.label: Error table · 5/8
steps.speakerNotes: For N equal 3, 5, 10 the maximum error is 0.866, 0.588, 0.309.

steps.label: Error table · 5/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: For N equal 20, 40, 80 it is 0.156, 0.0785, 0.0393. Doubling the neurons roughly halves the error.

steps.label: Error table · 5/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The reason: half a cell times the maximum slope 2 pi, which is pi over N. An error below 0.01 needs about 320 neurons. In higher dimensions it only gets worse.

steps.label: Error table · 5/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: \frac{1}{2N}\cdot2\pi=\frac{\pi}{N} half a cell times the maximum slope 2\pi; N=10: 0.309\approx\pi/10 an error below 0.01 needs about N\approx320: “enough” may really be a lot

steps.label: Proof skeleton · 6/8
steps.speakerNotes: Step one: define the hypothesis space and prove it is dense in the continuous functions, meaning any continuous function can be approximated by it.

steps.label: Proof skeleton · 6/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Step two: by contradiction assume it is not dense. By Hahn-Banach there is a nonzero continuous linear functional that vanishes on every function in the space.

steps.label: Proof skeleton · 6/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Step three: by Riesz representation this functional is an integral against some measure.

steps.label: Proof skeleton · 6/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Step four: the properties of sigma force the measure to be 0, contradicting nonzero, so the space is dense.

steps.label: Proof skeleton · 6/8 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: 4  contradiction continuous, bounded, nonconstant \sigma separates measures, forcing \mu=0, contradicting L\ne0 only the skeleton here; the details are functional analysis

steps.label: Guarantees and non-guarantees · 7/8
steps.speakerNotes: Guarantee: with enough neurons, a single-hidden-layer network has some parameters that approximate any continuous function to any accuracy.

steps.label: Guarantees and non-guarantees · 7/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Not promised: how large N must be, with the staircase example needing hundreds and more in high dimensions; nor how to find the parameters, which needs a learning algorithm, Chapter 3.

steps.label: Guarantees and non-guarantees · 7/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Nor that it does well on unseen data, which is KP04's generalization problem; nor that training reaches the global optimum.

steps.label: Guarantees and non-guarantees · 7/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: not promised: that it does well on unseen data (KP04's generalization) not promised: that training reaches the global optimum the theorem promises “a solution exists”, not “it can be found” or “it generalizes”

steps.label: Myths and next chapter · 8/8
steps.speakerNotes: First myth: the theorem guarantees a network can learn any function. No, it only says the parameters exist.

steps.label: Myths and next chapter · 8/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Second myth: the activation must be a sigmoid or bounded. This version assumes bounded; later work shows any non-polynomial works, even ReLU.

steps.label: Myths and next chapter · 8/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Third myth: many layers are needed for expressive power. One layer suffices for approximation; many layers usually need far fewer neurons.

steps.label: Myths and next chapter · 8/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Chapter 2 is done. How do these weights learn themselves, especially the hidden layers in a deep network that never see the answer? That is Chapter 3: backpropagation and gradient descent.

steps.label: Myths and next chapter · 8/8 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: We know what a network can represent. The real question: how do these weights learn themselves, especially the hidden layers in a deep network that never see the answer? Chapter 3: backpropagation and gradient descent
